intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that annular epidermolytic ichthyosis-1 (AEI1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding keratin-10 (KRT10).

checks.claim: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis-1 (AEI1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KRT10 gene, which encodes keratin-10.
checks.evidence_quote: Molecular analysis revealed a novel tandem CG to GA 2-bp mutation in the same allele of keratin 10 in affected individuals
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a KRT10 mutation in affected individuals and says inheritance is consistent with autosomal dominant transmission. It never explicitly says the mutation is heterozygous, and it reports only one family.

paragraphs.text: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a rare phenotypic variant of epidermolytic ichthyosis (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma). Affected individuals may have bullous ichthyosis in early life and hyperkeratotic plaques in flexural and extensor areas, and characteristically have recurrent bouts of annular, polycyclic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal extremities; palmoplantar keratoderma may be present. Histologic examination shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (Joh et al., 1997; Suga et al., 1998; Mikilita et al., 2020).

checks.evidence_quote: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis (AEI) is a rare phenotypic variant of epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI), also known as congenital bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma

paragraphs.text: Sahn et al. (1992) reported a 30-year-old white woman who developed bullous and ichthyosiform skin lesions at age 8 months. Blistering ceased at puberty, but hyperkeratotic plaques persisted. At age 27 years she developed numerous annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and extremities that were pruritic, enlarged slowly, and then resolved. Histopathologic examination of the annular plaques showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, and electron microscopy showed interrupted perinuclear tonofilament rings. Two of her 5 children were affected with a bullous type of ichthyosis.

paragraphs.text: Joh et al. (1997) reported a second family with annular epidermolytic ichthyosis, with 2 affected generations. The proband had bullous ichthyosis and bouts of disease activity associated with numerous annular and polycyclic erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and proximal extremities. Histologic examination showed the typical pathology of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, and ultrastructural analysis showed abnormal keratin filament networks and tonofilament clumping with a perinuclear distribution.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) reported an 8-year-old girl with diffuse dermatosis beginning in the first months of life. She had erythematous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with prominent borders on the mesogastrium, cubital and popliteal fossae, and inguinal and cervical regions, as well as palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and nasal introitus; hair, nails, and mucosa were unaffected. There was no family history of similar cases and no consanguinity. One month later the plaques had changed in appearance and extent, and the polycyclic aspect had disappeared. Skin biopsy showed acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis with marked epidermolysis in the granular layer. The initial diagnostic hypothesis had been erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva. In a review of the literature, the authors found 19 reported cases in 10 publications.

agent.process_note: I read all 4 papers in full. Three of them (Sahn 1992, Joh 1997, Suga 1998) are available only as abstracts. Mikilita 2020 is a full-text case report with a literature review. The causal gene, KRT10, comes from the Joh and Suga abstracts. Zygosity is inferred from Joh: it describes autosomal dominant inheritance and a 2-bp change on one allele. Suga does not state zygosity. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so I left out the KRT10 MIM number and chromosome location. I named the R83E variant by its 2B-segment residue number as Joh gives it, because no full-length codon number was available. I did not use the KRT1 mention in Mikilita for any mutation details, since no primary KRT1 paper was in the folder.
